items.q: Since the new library (A) has opened last spring, students (B) have been borrowing (C) far more books than the staff (D) expected.
items.explanation: A finished action with a definite past time (last spring) takes the past simple, not the present perfect; the present perfect belongs in the main clause after since.

items.q: Our chemistry teacher (A) explained that water (B) was boiling at a lower temperature (C) on high mountains because the air pressure (D) is lower there.
items.explanation: A scientific fact or general truth stays in the present simple even after a past reporting verb like explained.

items.q: The number of tourists (A) visiting the old town (B) each summer (C) have risen sharply since the new bridge (D) was completed in 2023.
items.explanation: The number of + plural noun is a singular subject, so the verb must be singular (has risen); only a number of takes a plural verb.

items.q: Although he was born in (A) the countryside, my uncle has lived (B) in Hanoi (C) for years and now works as (D) the lawyer in a big firm.
items.explanation: A job or profession introduced for the first time takes the indefinite article: work as a lawyer, be a teacher.

items.q: My grandmother is very (A) good in remembering birthdays, (B) even though she (C) has never written (D) a single one down.
items.explanation: The adjective good takes the preposition at before a skill or activity (good at remembering), never in.

items.q: The documentary (A) about coral reefs was so (B) interested that even my little brother, (C) who hates science, watched (D) the whole thing.
items.explanation: The -ing adjective describes the thing that causes the feeling (the documentary was interesting); the -ed form describes the person who feels it.

items.q: The old man (A) who lives next door grows vegetables (B) in his garden and often gives (C) some of it to (D) the children on our street.
items.explanation: A pronoun must agree with its antecedent: vegetables is plural, so it needs them, not it.

items.q: Travelling by train (A) across the country (B) takes longer than flying, (C) but it is (D) far more cheaper and much more relaxing.
items.explanation: A one-syllable adjective forms its comparative with -er alone; adding more as well (more cheaper) is a double comparative.

items.q: (A) If the river will rise any further tonight, the villagers (B) living near the bank (C) will have to move (D) to the school hall.
items.explanation: In a first conditional the if-clause uses the present simple; will appears only in the main clause.

items.q: When I asked where (A) the nearest bus stop was, the woman (B) said me that (C) it was just around (D) the corner.
items.explanation: Tell takes a direct object (told me) but say does not; you would need said to me or told me.

items.q: Last summer we stayed in a small village (A) in the mountains, (B) where the only shop (C) who sold bread also (D) served as the post office.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun who refers only to people; a thing such as a shop needs which or that.

items.q: The students were (A) so tired after the exam (B) that nobody (C) could remember (D) where had they parked their bikes.
items.explanation: An embedded (indirect) question keeps statement word order: subject before verb, with no inversion after where.

items.q: (A) There were too much people at the concert, so we (B) could hardly see the stage, (C) let alone (D) hear the singer clearly.
items.explanation: People is a plural countable noun, so it takes many; much is used only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: My father (A) refuses to buy a new phone (B) despite his old one (C) switches itself off (D) several times a day.
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form; a full clause with a subject and verb needs the conjunction even though or although.

items.q: Our teacher (A) reminded us to (B) finish the project on time and (C) make our best (D) in the presentation.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is do one's best; make does not combine with best.

items.q: By the time the firefighters (A) reached the warehouse, the flames (B) had already spread to (C) the roof, and thick smoke (D) is pouring out of the windows.
items.explanation: The whole sentence describes a past scene, so an action in progress at that moment takes the past continuous (was pouring), not the present.

items.q: (A) Each of the paintings in this room were (B) created by a local artist (C) who taught herself (D) to paint after retiring.
options: Each of the paintings in this room were
items.correction: Each of the paintings in this room was
items.explanation: Each of + plural noun is a singular subject and takes a singular verb (was created), whatever the noun after of.

items.q: Because my mother was afraid (A) of missing the flight, we (B) arrived to the airport three hours (C) before the plane (D) was due to leave.
items.explanation: Arrive is followed by at (a building or point) or in (a city or country), never by to.

items.q: During the trip to Da Lat, we visited (A) a strawberry farm, (B) tasted fresh milk and (C) played the football with (D) some local children.
items.explanation: Names of sports and games take no article after play: play football, play chess.

items.q: The new bakery on our street (A) has become popular (B) so quickly that (C) you often have to wait (D) patient in a long queue.
items.explanation: A word that describes how an action is done (wait) must be an adverb, so the adjective patient becomes patiently.

items.q: (A) Me and my classmates are planning to (B) raise money for the flood victims (C) by selling handmade cards (D) at the school fair.
items.explanation: The subject of a sentence needs the subject pronoun I, not the object pronoun me, and the speaker is placed last: My classmates and I.

items.q: Of all the planets in the solar system, Jupiter is (A) by far (B) the larger, (C) with a mass more than twice (D) that of all the others combined.
options: with a mass more than twice
items.explanation: Comparing one item with a whole group (of all the planets) requires the superlative the largest; the comparative is for two items only.

items.q: The head girl joked that (A) if she (B) were the principal, she (C) will cancel homework (D) for the whole of December.
items.explanation: If she were marks an unreal second conditional, so the main clause needs would + verb, not will.

items.q: The receptionist (A) explained that the museum (B) closed early on Mondays and (C) asked whether we (D) want to come back the following day.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb (asked) the verb in reported speech shifts back one tense: want becomes wanted.

items.q: (A) The photographer which took our family portrait (B) has been working (C) in the same studio (D) for nearly thirty years.
items.explanation: A person as the antecedent needs the relative pronoun who (or that); which is used only for things and animals.

items.q: My aunt (A) speaks (B) very well English because she (C) spent five years (D) studying and working in Canada.
items.explanation: An adverb of manner does not come between a verb and its object; the object (English) comes first, then very well.

items.q: While the volunteers (A) were cleaning the beach, they (B) found a turtle that (C) has been trapped in a fishing net (D) for several days.
items.explanation: An action that continued up to a point in the past (they found) takes the past perfect (continuous), not the present perfect.

items.q: Either the coach or the players (A) are going to (B) speak to reporters (C) after the final, (D) which start at seven o'clock.
items.explanation: The relative clause refers to the final, a singular noun, so its verb must be singular: which starts. (Are is correct because with either … or the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the players.)

items.q: (A) Little students in our class (B) have ever seen snow, so the trip to Sapa in January (C) was the most exciting event (D) of the year.
items.explanation: Few goes with plural countable nouns (few students); little is used only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: Many people (A) believe that (B) the succeed of a restaurant depends (C) more on service (D) than on the food itself.
items.explanation: After the article the and before of a noun is required, so the verb succeed must become the noun success.

items.q: The school orchestra (A) has been practising every evening (B) so that it will be ready (C) in the concert (D) at the end of term.
options: so that it will be ready
items.explanation: Ready is followed by for when it means prepared for an event (ready for the concert).

items.q: The farmers (A) believe that (B) if the dam had been built (C) ten years earlier, last summer's floods (D) would be far less serious.
options: if the dam had been built
items.correction: would have been far less serious
items.explanation: A third conditional about the past (had been built, last summer) needs would have + past participle in the main clause.

items.q: (A) I have visited my grandparents' farm last month (B) and was surprised (C) to see how much (D) the village had changed.
items.explanation: The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time expression such as last month; use the past simple.

items.q: Honestly, the second half of the film (A) was (B) much more boring as the first, (C) so we left (D) before the ending.
items.explanation: A comparative form (more boring) is followed by than; as belongs only to the pattern as … as.

items.q: One of the reasons (A) why so many teenagers (B) enjoy online games (C) are that they can (D) play with friends in other countries.
items.explanation: The head of the subject is one (one of the reasons), which is singular, so the main verb must be is.

items.q: Every summer we return to the little coastal town (A) in which my parents (B) first met, (C) and we always visit the café (D) that they had their first date.
options: that they had their first date
items.correction: where they had their first date
items.explanation: The clause already has its own object (their first date), so the café is a place, not an object, and needs the relative adverb where (or in which).

items.q: (A) In the end of the lesson, the teacher (B) handed back our essays and (C) praised those who (D) had used a wide range of vocabulary.
options: In the end of the lesson
items.correction: At the end of the lesson
items.explanation: At the end of refers to the final part of something; in the end means 'finally' and is never followed by of.

items.q: The first prize (A) was shared between (B) Minh and I, (C) although he had done (D) most of the work himself.
items.explanation: After a preposition (between) the object pronoun is required: between Minh and me, not I.

items.q: Scientists are still (A) trying to understand (B) why some birds can (C) navigation across oceans (D) without ever getting lost.
items.explanation: The modal can must be followed by a bare verb, so the noun navigation has to become the verb navigate.

items.q: My mother's recipe for pancakes (A) needs three eggs, (B) a cup of milk, (C) a pinch of salt and (D) a few flour.
items.explanation: Flour is uncountable, so it takes a little; a few is used only with plural countable nouns.
